newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court upholds key insider-trading law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court upholds key insider-trading law.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday upheld one of the federal government's toughest and most powerful enforcement weapons in fighting insider-trading abuses.

The high court by a 6-3 vote ruled that the government was correct in its interpretation of an important section of the securities law that makes it a crime for a person to use confidential information in securities trading.

Under the government's theory, if an individual misappropriates secret information and trades on it, it is illegal because the person has breached a trust or duty, even if the individual is not a traditional company insider.
The ruling reinstated the conviction of James O'Hagan, a Minneapolis lawyer whose firm had been retained by London-based Grand Metropolitan PLC over its 1988 takeover of Pillsbury Co.

O'Hagan was convicted of using secret information about the deal to reap a $4.3 million profit in Pillsbury stock and stock options, and was sentenced to 41 months in prison. His conviction had been overturned by a U.S. appeals court.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said for the court majority that a person who trades in securities for personal profit, using secret information misappropriated in breach of a duty to the source of the information, may be held liable for violating the securities law.
"Misappropriators deceive by pretending loyalty to a principal while secretly using the principal's information for personal gain," she said from the bench in summarizing the ruling.
Ginsburg emphasised that the law's purpose was "to insure honest securities markets, thereby promoting investor confidence."

She said it would make little sense, as the appeals court held, to hold O'Hagan liable if he had worked for a law firm representing the target of a tender offer, but not because he worked for a firm representing the bidder.

Ginsburg said the Securities and Exchange Commission did not exceed its authority by adopting a rule on insider trading involving tender offers, another part of the law under which O'Hagan had been convicted. She also upheld his mail fraud conviction.
The "misappropriation theory" of securities law at issue has been used by the government in a number of high-profile cases against people who were not considered company insiders.

Those cases include a printer of secret tender offer documents, a psychiatrist who learned from a patient of a takeover bid and former Wall Street Journal reporter R. Foster Winans, who leaked confidential information before it appeared in a widely read stocks column.

The U.S. Justice Department, on behalf of the SEC, warned that the appeals court ruling will "critically weaken the government's ability to prosecute the misuse of material, nonpublic information in the securities markets."

It said the appeals court decision "opened a large loophole in the protections against fraud afforded by federal law," and warned that it will hurt investor confidence in the integrity of the nation's securities markets.
According to the SEC, last year it took to court 42 cases of insider trading and began an additional 322 investigations into allegations of insider trading.
Dissenting from the main part of the ruling on the misappropriation theory were Chief Justice William Rehnquist, Clarence Thomas and Antonin Scalia.
"Because the (SEC's) misappropriation theory fails to provide a coherent and consistent interpretation for liability (under the securites law), I dissent," Thomas said.
Thomas also said he would strike down the SEC's inside-trading rule for tender offers, but added that he would uphold O'Hagan's mail fraud conviction.
